blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — sertraline late-pregnancy neonatal effects and monitoring
stem: A pregnant client taking sertraline asks why the newborn may need observation after third-trimester exposure. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

options.A: Late-pregnancy sertraline exposure can be associated with neonatal respiratory, feeding, or neurologic adaptation problems, so the newborn should be observed for those possible effects.
options.B: Third-trimester sertraline exposure predictably causes severe neonatal toxicity requiring prolonged hospitalization and respiratory support in essentially every exposed newborn.
options.C: Sertraline exposure late in pregnancy has not been associated with neonatal respiratory, feeding, neurologic, or pulmonary complications, so newborn observation is unnecessary.
options.D: The main neonatal concern after third-trimester sertraline exposure is a congenital limb deformity present at birth rather than postnatal respiratory or adaptation symptoms.

rationale: Current ZOLOFT (sertraline) labeling states that exposure to SSRIs and SNRIs, including sertraline, in late pregnancy may increase the risk of neonatal complications requiring respiratory support or tube feeding and/or persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Reported findings after late third-trimester exposure include respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, jitteriness, and other neurologic or autonomic findings. The label directs clinicians to monitor third-trimester-exposed neonates for PPHN and drug discontinuation syndrome. These outcomes are possible rather than inevitable, so A is correct. B converts a reported risk into a near-universal outcome, C contradicts the labeled neonatal risks, and D substitutes an unsupported congenital-limb-defect claim.
educational_objective: Teach that late-pregnancy sertraline exposure can be associated with neonatal respiratory, feeding, and neurologic adaptation symptoms and warrants newborn monitoring without implying that every exposed infant will be severely affected.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA labeling
source_document_title: ZOLOFT (sertraline hydrochloride) tablets and oral solution — Full Prescribing Information
source_version_date: DailyMed drug label updated August 8, 2023; current label verified and accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Use in Specific Populations §8.1 Pregnancy — Fetal/Neonatal Adverse Reactions and Data > Human Data > Third Trimester Exposure: monitor third-trimester-exposed neonates for PPHN and drug discontinuation syndrome; reported complications include respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, and jitteriness.
source_claim_supported: Late-pregnancy sertraline/SSRI exposure may be associated with neonatal complications including respiratory distress, feeding difficulty, tremor, jitteriness, and PPHN; third-trimester-exposed neonates should be monitored for PPHN and drug discontinuation syndrome.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: educate client about medications; evaluate client response to medication; review pertinent data and adverse effects.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as substantive neonatal-risk explanations without absolute-word distractor cues.
Balanced option length and preserved risk language as possible rather than inevitable, eliminating the original unsupported precision and cueing.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches current sertraline labeling and correctly uses nonabsolute risk language. All options are closely length-matched; B overstates risk, C denies documented neonatal effects, and D substitutes an unsupported congenital-defect claim.
